newsitem.title: UK: The strong dollar fuels volatility in commodities.
newsitem.headline: The strong dollar fuels volatility in commodities.

text.p: A strong dollar fuelled volatility in commodity markets, giving the gold price another kick down on Wednesday, but it may take some heat out of a potential new trade spat between the United States and Europe over grain subsidies.

The dollar's rise in value of more than 7-1/2 percent since January 1, measured against a trade-weighted basket of currencies, is good news for some exporters of raw materials, on which most prices are set in dollars.
"OPEC will breathe a sigh of relief if the dollar continues to strengthen,' said Geoff Pyne, an energy economist with UBS.

Gold sank to a new 3-3/4 year low at $336.50 an ounce on Wednesday, extending a sharp decline mainly on fears that other central banks may follow a recent Dutch example and sell bullion from their reserves.
A strong dollar adds to the pressure on gold by propping its value in the currencies of nations outside the United States - when jittery speculators then grab the chance to bale out.
The dollar rally may reduce the risk of new trade tension between the European Union and the US over export subsidies as the EU battles to stay competitive on weakening world grain markets.

A firm dollar means the EU can afford to pay lower subsidies in European currency units to make up the difference between the price at which its farmers can afford to produce and a world price set in the dollar.
"It puts Brussels at ease," a UK exporter said. "A strong dollar means that the same dollar price gives a bigger European price."
Even so, in a weakening world market, the EU raised subsidies by some 3.0 percent last week as it tried to sell a near-record harvest.
US Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman has resisted pressure to retaliate but says he cannot ignore EU subsidies indefinitely.
Some traders also think that, in practice, Europe may just end up exporting more wheat at the same subsidy. Exporters who saw the EU happy with 200-250,000 tonnes of wheat a week now look for a rise.
Benchmark crude oil prices are down to just above $20 per barrel from a post-Gulf War high at $25 seen in October.
The oil market has eased now that the United Nations Gulf War ban on Iraqi exports has been relaxed and seasonal US and European winter demand for heating fuel to replenish low stocks has abated.
The Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries can expect the strong dollar to ease the pinch as crude values drop.
For some, however, led by Venezuela and Saudi Arabia, the benefit is somewhat offset by the volume of their dollar-denominated imports.
Trade data shows Libya gains most. It is under US sanctions and most of its imports are in currencies other than the dollar.

Analysts add, however, that energy consumers outside the US ought not to take a big inflationary hit from a strong dollar. Taxes and profit margins, not the cost of crude, make up most of the pump price of fuel.

But the appreciating dollar was cited in recent days by German coffee roasters, along with a dramatic rise in the world price of beans which is also set in dollars, when they raised supermarket prices for coffees.

Coffee prices have soared by 40 percent since early January in a speculative rally triggered by prospects that Brazil may have a lower-than-expected crop, labour unrest in Colombia and a view that stocks are low.
Third World sellers of coffee can look for an extra bonus from the strength of the dollar.

Industrial metals prices, also set in dollars, have rallied this year, adding to raw material costs to industry in several nations. Nickel is up 20 percent since the end of 1996 and zinc by 12 percent.
But copper and aluminium, the traded metals that are most extensively used, have advanced modestly.
